summary: Recommends that routers stop forwarding directed broadcasts by default, which helps prevent attacks that use a network to flood a victim. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If you shout a message to a whole street from outside, one trick can make everyone shout back at a victim. Routers are told not to pass such shouts along unless asked.

subtitle: Routers should ignore directed broadcasts unless an administrator turns them on.

tldr.problem: RFC 1812 required routers to forward directed broadcasts by default, and on the Internet backbone their use appeared to consist entirely of malicious attacks on other networks.
tldr.mechanism: This memo replaces two passages of RFC 1812 so that receiving and forwarding network-prefix-directed broadcasts is optional and must be disabled by default.
tldr.outcome: Newly deployed routers no longer add to the Smurf amplifier problem unless the operator deliberately enables the feature.

facts.label: New default
facts.value: Receiving and forwarding of directed broadcasts blocked

today: RFC 2644 is Best Current Practice 34 and updates RFC 1812. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem With the Old Default
sections.content:
Router Requirements (RFC 1812) said routers must receive and forward directed broadcasts. It also said routers MUST have an option to disable this, but that the option MUST default to permitting them.

The author notes that directed broadcasts have uses, yet on the Internet backbone their use appears to be comprised entirely of malicious attacks on other networks. Changing the required default would help ensure new routers connected to the Internet do not add to the problems already present.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said routers must pass these big shouts along by default. Almost the only people using them on the big Internet were attackers.

sections.title: Smurf Attacks and Amplifiers
sections.content:
Damaging denial of service attacks led to the writing of RFC 2267 on Ingress Filtering. A recent trend in Smurf Attacks is to target networks that permit directed broadcasts from outside their networks. By permitting them, those systems become Smurf Amplifiers.

Ingress filtering remains the best way to limit these attacks, but restricting directed broadcasts should also receive priority. Network service providers and corporate network operators are urged to ensure their networks are not susceptible to directed broadcast packets originating outside their networks.

The memo also mentions that Mobile IP (RFC 2002) had provisions for directed broadcasts in dynamic agent discovery. It is unclear whether that is useful, and the text suggests it may be worthwhile to consider removing that language.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers send one shout to a network that echoes it to everyone, and all the echoes land on a victim. A network that allows the shout is helping the attacker without meaning to.

sections.title: The New Router Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4.2.2.11 (d) of RFC 1812 is replaced. A directed broadcast of the form { <Network-prefix>, -1 } MUST NOT be used as a source address. A router MAY originate such packets. A router MAY have a configuration option to receive them, but that option MUST be disabled by default, so the router MUST NOT receive them unless the end user configures it.

The second paragraph of section 5.3.5.2 is also replaced. A router MAY have options to enable receiving and forwarding network-prefix-directed broadcasts on an interface, and these options MUST default to blocking receipt and blocking forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers now start with the door shut. A person has to switch the feature on on purpose before the router will pass the big shouts along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The whole point of the memo is security. The goal stated in the RFC is to reduce the efficacy of certain types of denial of service attacks. No other considerations are listed.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is simple: make it harder for bad guys to use other people's networks to flood someone.
